about: Every character a record, a rank file or a species' spec may state (growth plan G2.2, and the characters of the spec rework): its group, the organ it describes, its type and its unit, values or range. Vocabulary only: the rules that turn characters into spec values live in the taxa they hold for. Types: number (a quantity in its unit), count (a whole number), bool, enum (one of its values), enums (a list of its values), months (a list of months, 1 to 12), colour (sRGB, three numbers 0 to 255), text (a line in PlantGen's own words), ids (species ids). A number or count may instead be a range, {"min": 5, "max": 8}, with the rare extremes beyond it as `low` and `high` and the most usual value as `typical`: a flora's (3-)5-8 is {"min": 5, "max": 8, "low": 3}. A range says how the plant varies, not how sure a source is. An enum or bool may instead be qualified, each state with how often it occurs (usually, often, sometimes, rarely): usually opposite, rarely alternate is {"opposite": "usually", "alternate": "rarely"}. Organs are the parts characters describe, from the thallus of a seaweed to the bark of a tree; each but the whole plant is part of another, and each has a category from `categories`: the whole plant, an axis, an organ, a group or a tissue. An organ may be one of a kind from `kinds` (`is_a`), as each kind of floret is a floret, and a character of the kind applies wherever an organ of that kind exists. Where the Plant Ontology has a term for the same structure, `po` names it, from the release `po_release`. An organ with a `when` exists only where one of those characters takes one of the values listed (a qualified value counts with each of its states, and a character that cannot apply takes none of them), and its characters apply only there; a character's own `when` narrows it further, as leaves_per_whorl applies only to whorled leaves. A character with `at_most` is never above the one it names, as a typical height is never above the greatest. A character marked `optional` is one many plants have nothing to state for, and the audit never counts it missing.

categories.whole: the whole plant, which every other organ is part of
categories.axis: a body that grows at its tips and may branch, bearing other parts along it: roots, a stem, a thallus, rhizoids
categories.organ: a part of limited growth, borne whole: a leaf, a flower or floret, a fruit, a seed, a spore capsule, a holdfast
categories.group: parts packed together on a shared axis or base and seen as one: an inflorescence, a head, a spikelet, a cone, a sorus
categories.tissue: a layer of another part, such as bark

plant.why: the whole plant: its form, size, life and where it grows

root.why: the roots, which grow underground to anchor the plant and take up water

rhizoid.why: a thread of one cell or a row of cells that holds a plant without roots to its ground, as in mosses, liverworts, hornworts and stoneworts

holdfast.why: the disc, cushion or tangle of threads that holds a seaweed to rock or shell

stem.why: the shoots that bear leaves, flowers and cones, and the wood they lay down; a moss's or leafy liverwort's stem among them

thallus.why: a body not divided into stem and leaves: the forking ribbon of a thalloid liverwort or hornwort, or the blades, branches, threads or crusts of an alga

bark.why: the outer layer of a woody stem

leaf.why: a leaf from its stalk to its tip; a fern's frond, a grass's blade and a moss's leaf are leaves

leaflet.why: one of the separate blades of a compound leaf

sorus.why: a cluster of sporangia on a fern's leaf, on its underside or along its edge

areole.why: a cactus's short, felted bud at a node, on a rib, a tubercle or a joint's face, from which its spines, glochids, flowers and branches come

spine.why: a hard, sharp point that arms a plant, whichever organ it is made from (the spines character says which): a thorn, a shoot (PO:0025172); a prickle, from the bark's skin (PO:0025169); a leaf, stipule or leaf stalk turned spine (PO:0025173, PO:0025174, PO:0025613); or a cactus's spines from an areole. The Plant Ontology has no one term for them all

inflorescence.why: a flowering shoot: how flowers, heads or spikelets are grouped

flower.why: a single flower, where single flowers make up the inflorescence

sepal.why: one of the outer whorl of a flower whose perianth is sepals and petals, its calyx; usually green

petal.why: one of the inner whorl of a flower whose perianth is sepals and petals, its corolla

tepal.why: a perianth part where sepals and petals are alike, in two whorls (lilies, irises) or on a spiral (water lilies, cacti)

stamen.why: a filament and the anther it bears, where pollen forms

staminode.why: a sterile stamen, with no anther or a barren one; a stamen that is absent is not one

carpel.why: one unit of a flower's pistil, its ovary bearing ovules; free, or joined with others in one pistil

capitulum.why: a head: florets packed on a shared receptacle inside a ring of bracts (phyllaries), as in the daisy family

ray_floret.why: a floret at the rim of a radiate head, its corolla drawn out into a strap (lamina)

disc_floret.why: a floret in the middle of a head, its corolla a small tube

ligulate_floret.why: a floret of a head made only of strap-shaped florets, as in dandelions

phyllary.why: one of the bracts in rows round a head's foot, its involucre

inflorescence_bract.why: a bract at the foot of an inflorescence or on its axis: an aroid's spathe, a dogwood's petal-like bracts, an umbel's involucre

spikelet.why: the unit of grasses and sedges: florets on a small axis, in grasses above a pair of glumes

glume.why: one of the empty bracts at a spikelet's foot, below its florets

spikelet_floret.why: a small flower of a spikelet, held by its lemma (a sedge's by its scale)

awn.why: the stiff bristle a spikelet floret's lemma ends in or bears on its back

fruit.why: a ripe fruit, from a flower or floret

cone.why: a cone (strobilus): scales packed on a short axis at a shoot's tip, bearing seeds (a conifer's seed cone) or spores (the cone of a horsetail or clubmoss)

seed.why: a seed borne alone on a shoot, outside any fruit or cone, often in a fleshy cup or coat: the yew's aril, the ginkgo's outer coat

capsule.why: the spore capsule of a moss, liverwort or hornwort, which grows from the plant and sheds its spores; a hornwort's is a long green horn

floret.why: a small flower packed with others in a head; each kind of floret is a floret, and a character of the floret applies wherever one of them does

library_form.why: Library 1.0's nine classes, for search and its quotas per class

growth_form.why: the spec's growth forms, which pick a rank file's part for its form

reproduction.why: how it bears seeds or spores: seeds in fruit from flowers, seeds open on the scales of cones, seeds borne singly or in pairs outside any cone (yews, ginkgo), or spores and no seeds

body_plan.why: what the plant's body is built of: stems and leaves with veins (ferns, horsetails, clubmosses and seed plants), a small leafy shoot without veins (mosses and leafy liverworts), a thallus not divided into stem and leaves (thalloid liverworts, hornworts and most seaweeds), or single cells, alone or in colonies

anchorage.why: what holds the plant to its ground: roots; rhizoids, threads of one cell or a row of cells (mosses, liverworts, hornworts, stoneworts); a holdfast at a seaweed's foot; or nothing, where it floats or hangs free

leaf_bearing.why: whether a plant with stems bears leaves: false where it has none, as in most cacti, whose spines stand in for them

sporangia.why: where a plant that spreads by spores bears its sporangia: in sori on its leaves (most ferns), in cones at the tips of its shoots (horsetails, most clubmosses), or in a capsule that grows from the plant (mosses, liverworts, hornworts)

leaf_habit.why: how long leaves stay on through the year

life_span.why: how many years a plant lives and sets seed in

clonal.why: whether it spreads by its own shoots, runners or roots

rhizome_habit.why: how a plant's rhizome grows, where it has one: upright or rising under a crown, creeping a little so the plant forms a clump, or running far underground so it forms a colony

perennation.why: what a perennial herb lasts the bad season in underground (or, for a pseudobulb, a swollen stem above it): a bulb or a corm usually sends up one flowering stem of its own, a rhizome or tubers a clump of them; how a rhizome grows is `rhizome_habit`, so a plant that perennates in a rhizome has one other than none

habit_notes.why: what the other form traits leave unsaid

crown_width_max_m.why: the widest a crown or clump grows

crown_outline_fit.why: how nearly a grown, open-grown crown's outline seen from the side is an ellipse: its intersection over union with the ellipse of the same area and second moments, 1 for an ellipse (crown form research, 2026-10-12); a lobed, flat-topped or vase-shaped crown fits less

crown_see_through.why: the share of a grown, open-grown crown's outline seen from the side that the sky shows through, between its leaves, its wood and its lobes

culm_length_m.why: a grass's, sedge's or rush's flowering culm, its length as floras give it, which may be more than its height where it leans or bends at a node

stem_diameter_max_m.why: the thickest a stem grows, at breast height for trees

juvenile_period_years.why: the years from germination to a plant's first flowers or cones (its juvenile period)

thallus_form.why: the shape a thallus grows in: a flat ribbon forking as it grows (thalloid liverworts, hornworts), a thin blade or sheet (sea lettuce, nori), a bush of branches (stoneworts, most red seaweeds), threads (filamentous algae), or a crust on rock or shell (coralline algae)

thallus_length_m.why: a grown thallus, from its base or oldest part to its farthest tip

branching.why: the crown's habit: a leading stem, a spreading one, a column, canes or none

crown_form.why: the outline of a grown, open-grown crown seen from the side: a dome, wider than tall on arching limbs, flat-topped, narrow below and wide above, a cone, a column, hanging, or none of these. It is the shape, where branching is the axes' habit that grows it: an excurrent tree is usually conical and a decurrent one rounded or spreading, and branching columnar goes with crown_form columnar

bark_texture.why: the bark of a grown stem

bark_colour.why: the bark of a grown stem

spines.why: what a plant is armed with: spines from areoles, thorns from shoots, prickles from bark, or spines on its leaves

stem_form.why: what a cactus's stem is built as: a column or a barrel growing on at its tip, or a chain of joints, cylindrical (a cholla's) or flattened into pads (a prickly pear's)

stem_cross_section.why: a stem's or culm's shape in cross-section: round, ridged or angled, three-angled (a sedge's culm), four-angled (a mint's), winged, or flattened

ribs.why: ribs running down a cactus's stem, its areoles along their crests; 0 where its areoles sit on tubercles or scattered over its joints

tubercles.why: whether a cactus's areoles sit on tubercles, knobs of the stem, alone (a pincushion's) or along its ribs

joint_length_m.why: a grown joint of a cholla or a prickly pear's pad, from its foot to its tip

joint_width_m.why: a grown joint's thickness across, or a pad's width at its widest

areole_spacing_m.why: from one areole to the next along a rib, or between neighbours on a joint

glochids.why: whether the areoles bear glochids, tufts of fine barbed bristles that come away at a touch (chollas and prickly pears)

radial_spines.why: spines round an areole's edge, spreading flat or nearly so; where a flora does not tell radials from centrals, all of them

central_spines.why: spines standing out from an areole's middle, usually stouter than the radials

radial_spine_length_m.why: the longest radial spines (or the longest spines, where a flora does not tell them apart)

central_spine_form.why: the main central spine's form: straight, curved, hooked at its tip (a fishhook's), flattened, or twisted

spine_sheaths.why: whether each spine wears a papery sheath, as a cholla's do

stem_colour.why: a green stem's skin, as a cactus's or a leafless shrub's, where no bark covers it

central_spine_colour.why: the central spines' colour where a flora gives it apart from the radials'

spine_colour_aged.why: an old spine's colour, once it has greyed or darkened

spine_colour.why: a grown spine's colour before it greys

wood_density_basic_kg_m3.why: the basic density of the stem's wood: its oven-dry mass over its green volume, as wood-density databases give it (the specific gravity times 1000)

wood_moisture_green_share.why: the water in living (green) wood as a share of its oven-dry mass, sapwood and heartwood together; green wood weighs its basic density times one plus this

wood_modulus_green_mpa.why: the modulus of elasticity of green wood in static bending: how stiff a living stem or branch is, its bending stiffness this times the section's second moment of area

wood_rupture_green_mpa.why: the modulus of rupture of green wood in static bending: the stress at which a living stem or branch breaks, its breaking moment this times the section modulus

leaf_form.why: what a leaf is made as: a flat blade (a fern's frond and a grass's leaf among them), a needle or a scale

leaf_division.why: whether the blade is one piece, however deeply cut, or made of separate leaflets

leaf_incision.why: how deeply a simple blade is cut: not at all, into lobes, to about halfway, most of the way, or into fine segments

division_pattern.why: how a compound leaf's leaflets or a cut blade's lobes are set: along a midrib, or from one point

division_order.why: how many times the leaflets or lobes divide: 1 once (pinnate), 2 twice (bipinnate)

leaf_shape.why: a blade's outline, or a compound leaf's leaflets'

leaf_venation.why: how the main veins run: from a midrib, from the base, side by side, forking in pairs, or one vein alone

leaf_arrangement.why: leaves at each node: one (alternate), a pair (opposite) or three or more (whorled)

leaves_per_whorl.why: leaves at each node of a whorled shoot

phyllotaxis_pattern.why: how each leaf node turns from the last: by about the golden angle (spiral), half a turn (distichous, two ranks), a third of a turn (tristichous, three ranks), or half the gap between its own leaves (decussate: pairs crossing, whorls alternating)

divergence_deg.why: the angle between successive leaf nodes, where a source measures it

rosette.why: leaves crowded on short internodes: not at all, at the base, or at the tips of stems

leaf_mass_fresh_kg_m2.why: the fresh (living) mass of a leaf per square metre of its one-sided area, its water included: the load leaves put on the branches that hold them

leaf_length_m.why: a grown leaf's blade, without its petiole

leaf_width_m.why: a grown leaf's blade at its widest

petiole_length_m.why: the stalk between blade and shoot

vernation.why: how a young leaf lies in the bud: coiled from its tip downward (circinate, a fern's fiddlehead), folded along its midrib, rolled in from its edges, or flat

leaf_life_years.why: how long a leaf lives from unfolding to falling: under one for a deciduous leaf, several for a fir's needles

frond_dimorphism.why: whether a fern's fertile and sterile leaves differ: alike, wholly different (a deer fern's erect, narrow fertile fronds), or differing only in the fertile part of each leaf

fertile_share.why: the share of a fertile blade, from its tip down, that bears sori

leaf_margin.why: a blade's edge: smooth, or toothed (teeth pointing forward, outward, rounded, or ending in spines)

leaflets.why: leaflets on a compound leaf, or on each pinna of a twice-divided one, as floras count them (a flora's pairs of leaflets are twice as many)

leaflet_length_m.why: a grown leaflet's blade, or a fern's pinna, the longest on the leaf, without its stalk

leaflet_width_m.why: a grown leaflet's blade, or a fern's pinna, at its widest

pinnae.why: the pinnae of a twice-divided leaf: its primary divisions, each bearing leaflets of its own (a mesquite's one or two pairs)

cauline_leaves.why: the leaves of a herb's flowering stem, as floras describe them: like those at its foot, reduced (fewer and smaller up the stem), or none, a leafless scape from the leaves at its foot

leaf_faces.why: whether a blade has an upper and a lower face, or is unifacial, its one face all round: a sword leaf flattened edgewise to the stem (irises) or a round one (onions, rushes)

leaf_peltation.why: where the petiole meets the blade: at its basal margin, the blade going on in its plane; at the margin, the blade held flat across the petiole's tip (latently peltate); or under the blade, inside its outline, like an umbrella (manifestly peltate)

terminal_leaflet.why: whether a pinnate leaf, and each pinna of a twice-pinnate one, ends in a single leaflet (odd-pinnate) rather than a pair (even-pinnate)

foliage_ranks.why: how a conifer's needles stand on a shoot: out all round it, or spread into two flat ranks, often by a twist at their base though they are set in a spiral (a yew's, a hemlock's)

stipules.why: whether leaves bear stipules at their base

leaf_colour.why: a grown leaf's upper side in summer

inflorescence.why: how the units of a flowering shoot are grouped: L1's cluster kinds, a single unit, or a spadix

inflorescence_unit.why: what an inflorescence is made of: single flowers, heads of florets (the daisy family) or spikelets (grasses and sedges)

units_per_inflorescence.why: the flowers, heads or spikelets in one inflorescence

inflorescence_branches.why: the primary branches of a compound inflorescence, each bearing units or branches of its own: a compound umbel's rays, a panicle's branches

inflorescence_posture.why: how an inflorescence holds itself: upright, bent over near its tip, or hanging

inflorescence_length_m.why: an inflorescence from its lowest unit or branch to its tip

peduncle_length_m.why: the bare stalk an inflorescence stands on, from where it leaves its shoot to its lowest unit or branch

inflorescence_bracts.why: bracts at the foot of an inflorescence: an aroid's one spathe, a dogwood's four, an umbel's involucre

bract_form.why: what those bracts are: one sheathing the inflorescence's foot and hooding it, showy like petals, green like leaves, or small scales

bract_length_m.why: the longest of those bracts, from its foot to its tip, a spathe's sheath included

petal_length_m.why: a petal from its base to its tip, claw included

sepal_length_m.why: a sepal from its base to its tip, or a joined calyx's lobe with its tube

pedicel_length_m.why: a flower's own stalk in a cluster, from the axis that bears it to the flower

flower_merosity.why: petals (or tepals) in one whorl of a flower

flower_symmetry.why: a flower's symmetry: radial, one plane, or none

perianth.why: what surrounds a flower's stamens: a calyx of sepals and a corolla of petals, two like whorls of tepals, tepals on a spiral, or nothing

perianth_parts.why: the tepals in all of a flower whose perianth is a spiral

corolla_shape.why: how a corolla is formed: spreading flat, a cup, a bell, a funnel, a tube, a narrow tube with a flat limb, or an urn narrowed at its mouth

zygomorphy.why: how a zygomorphic flower's parts differ by place: a pea flower's banner, wings and keel; two lips; an orchid's lip and column; or otherwise

hypanthium.why: whether a floral cup, the bases of the sepals, petals and stamens grown together, bears them above the receptacle (roses, currants)

ovary_position.why: where the ovary sits: above where the other whorls leave the receptacle, half below it, or below it, the whorls standing on its top

resupinate.why: whether the flower turns half round as it opens, so a lip formed on its upper side hangs below, as in most orchids

spur_length_m.why: a hollow spur at a petal's or lip's base, where there is one

anther_attachment.why: where the filament joins the anther: at its base, so the anther stands along the filament; on its back; or at one point on its back, so the anther swings free across the filament's tip

staminodes.why: the sterile stamens in one flower, where it has any

carpels.why: the carpels in one flower, free or joined

capitulum_kind.why: the florets a head holds: rays round a disc, a disc alone, a disc ringed by threadlike florets, or strap-shaped florets alone

involucre_diameter_m.why: the ring of phyllaries across, which floras give as a head's size

involucre_height_m.why: the ring of phyllaries from the head's foot to the tips of the inner ones, which floras give before its width (involucres 3-4 x 2-4 cm)

phyllary_series.why: the rows the phyllaries stand in

receptacle.why: whether chaffy scales (paleae) stand among a head's florets

receptacle_shape.why: the receptacle's profile under the florets: flat, gently domed, a half sphere or a cone

pappus.why: what tops the fruit of a head's florets: nothing, bristles, scales, awns or a small crown

pappus_length_m.why: the pappus's longest bristles or scales

ray_florets.why: the ray florets of one head

ray_width_m.why: a ray's strap (lamina), its width where widest

ray_apex.why: a ray's tip: narrowing to a point, rounded, cut square, or square with two or three small teeth

disc_florets.why: the disc florets of one head

ligulate_florets.why: the strap-shaped florets of one head

florets_per_spikelet.why: the fertile florets of one spikelet

spikelet_length_m.why: a spikelet from its base to the tip of its last floret, awns left out

glumes.why: the empty bracts at a spikelet's base

awns.why: whether its florets' lemmas end in an awn, a stiff bristle

awn_length_m.why: the awn on a floret's lemma

awn_insertion.why: where a lemma's awn leaves it: at its tip, just below the tip (often between two teeth), from the middle of its back, or near its base

awn_form.why: an awn's shape: straight, wavy, bent at a knee (geniculate), curved into a hook, or twisted and curled

upper_glume_length_m.why: a spikelet's upper (second) glume, from its base to its tip, awn left out; the only glume where there is one

lower_glume_length_m.why: a spikelet's lower (first) glume, awn left out

lemma_length_m.why: the lemma of a fertile floret, the bract that holds it, awn left out; in a sedge, the scale under a flower

scale_arrangement.why: how a spikelet's glumes and lemmas (a sedge's scales) stand on its axis: in two ranks, each on the other side from the one below, or in a spiral

sexual_system.why: where the sexes sit: in a dioecious species only half the plants bear fruit or seed cones

fruit_type.why: what a fruit is (pod for dry pods that split other than a legume; cypsela for the achene of the daisy family)

fruit_size_m.why: a ripe fruit at its longest

fruit_width_m.why: a ripe fruit across at its widest

fruiting_months.why: the months its fruit is ripe in

fruit_posture.why: how a ripe fruit or fruit cluster holds itself on its stalk: standing up, out to the side, bent down, or hanging (a lime's or an ash's keys), as cone_posture is for a seed cone

cone_width_m.why: a ripe seed cone across at its widest, closed

pollen_cone_length_m.why: a pollen (microsporangiate) cone when it sheds its pollen; cone_length_m is the seed cone's

cone_posture.why: how a seed cone sits on its shoot: standing up (a fir's), out to the side, bent down, or hanging (a spruce's)

cone_maturation_years.why: the seasons a seed cone takes from pollination to ripe: one for a spruce, two for most pines

cone_retention_years.why: how long a ripe cone stays on the tree once it has shed its seed: none where it falls apart on the branch (a fir's), many where it stays shut or hangs on (a shore pine's)

seed_length_m.why: a ripe seed with its aril or fleshy coat

seed_colour_ripe.why: a ripe seed as it is seen: its aril or fleshy coat where it has one

sorus_shape.why: a sorus's outline: a round dot, a short oblong or hook, a line along a vein or the midrib, or a band along the leaf's edge

indusium.why: what covers a young sorus: nothing, a kidney-shaped flap, a round shield on a central stalk, a flap along one side, or the leaf's own edge rolled over it

sorus_position.why: where on a pinna or segment its sori sit: beside its midrib, about halfway to its edge, near the edge, or on it

sori_rows.why: rows of sori on each side of a pinna's or segment's midrib

capsule_length_m.why: a ripe capsule, or a hornwort's horn, from base to tip

seta.why: whether a stalk, the seta, lifts the capsule above the plant, as in most mosses and liverworts; a hornwort's horn grows straight from the thallus

seta_length_m.why: the seta, from the plant to the capsule

leaf_out_months.why: the months new leaves unfold in

light.why: the light it grows in, every class it spans

moisture.why: the water its ground holds, every class it spans

soil_texture.why: the ground it roots in, every class it spans

habitat_notes.why: what the other ecology traits leave unsaid

hosts.why: the species a climber, epiphyte or parasite grows on

nurse_forms.why: the forms its seedlings need to shelter under

nurse_species.why: the species its seedlings need to shelter under

litter_kind.why: the ground look its litter makes

self_pruning.why: whether it sheds its own shaded limbs

architectural_model.why: the Halle-Oldeman model its growth follows: a label for search, set by each lineage, never a program

axis_growth.why: whether an axis grows on from its own tip or is carried on by a lateral

flowering_position.why: whether flowers end a shoot or sit beside its leaves

short_shoots.why: whether it grows long shoots and short ones (spurs)

bud_position.why: where along a year's shoot the buds that grow into long shoots sit: near its tip (acrotonic, most trees), in its middle (mesotonic), or near its foot (basitonic, many shrubs, which renew from their base)

shoot_leaves.why: the leaves a vigorous long shoot bears in one year's growth (its growth unit), from its foot to its tip

epicormic.why: whether dormant buds under the bark of old limbs and the trunk sprout into new shoots where light reaches them (delayed reiteration)

ramification_order.why: branch orders a grown crown carries
